Tracking QA — the distributions, run by run and tag by tag

14,263,041 gated tracks · 36 runs · 292 sub-runs · 3,232 file tags · generated 2026-09-10T10:17:15

Three things this found that a median could not.

  • Roughly one gated track in 3 carries a charge that cannot be real. 29.3 % of tracks have q_total above 106 ADC — worst on chamber D at 36.2 % — and the 95th percentile reaches 1014–1017 on a 12-bit ADC sitting on a ~330-count pedestal. q_total is x_q_sum + y_q_sum and both plane sums diverge together, so this is the fit's amplitude solution running away on some depth bins, not a units error. Their χ2 is unremarkable, which is why nothing caught it: the waveform still fits. Every charge-based statement in this analysis — gain comparisons, q_per_len, the charge window k_arm cuts on — runs on a column with a tail of garbage that large.
  • Chamber A fits its own model better than any other chamber. Its lower quartile of χ2/dof is 1.55, against B 7.12, C 4.82, D 2.64; medians 6.3 against 14.9, 12.2, 16.9. This is the same split that shows up in the angle scale: A is also the arm whose k varies least run to run. One fact, not two.
  • The 27 July access is a step, and separating it changes what counts as a trend. Correlating any variable against time across the whole campaign scores that step as a strong monotone trend, so this reports ρ before and after it separately. The strongest surviving post-access trend is chamber D's chi2dof_y (ρ = +0.57, p = 4e-252, over 2,987 tags), moving 20.1 before the access to 29.5 in the last tenth of the campaign.

The clearest outliers are already understood. The runs with the most flags are run_126 (10), run_79 (5), run_156 (5). run_79 and run_81 are the pre-access condition, when chamber A's x-view connector was dead; a run that fails to certify an angle scale flags on everything downstream of it. Both are checks that this method finds what it should, not new results.

Why this exists

Every tracking number quoted in this analysis so far has been a median over the whole campaign. A median cannot tell a chamber that is uniformly mediocre from one that is fine for most of the campaign and catastrophic for two hours on a Tuesday, and the second is the case worth finding. The angle scale k is measured to move 13–17 % between runs with nothing in the configuration to explain it, so the question here is whether anything in the reconstruction itself moves with it.

Nothing here cuts, corrects or reweights. An outlier below is a lead, not a verdict.

Does the drift span fit inside the chamber?

A bound on the angle scale that owes nothing to the pointing estimators, and therefore checks them. The reconstruction turns the fitted drift end time into a depth with v = 42.6/k, and the depth grid stops at 18 × 60 = 1080 ns, so the deepest span it can produce is fixed once k is. That span has to fit in the drift gap.

Chambers B, D pass. Chambers A, C do not — A: 68 % of its gated tracks reconstruct deeper than its 27.9 mm gap, with a median unrailed span of 29.3 mm and a scale of 1.229 against the 1.649 the gap demands; and C: 40 % of its gated tracks reconstruct deeper than its 30.0 mm gap, with a median unrailed span of 27.2 mm and a scale of 1.436 against the 1.534 the gap demands.

Two readings, both calibration faults, and this test cannot choose between them. Either the angle scale is too small on the failing arms, or their depth-grid origin sits outside the gas so the span is inflated with k innocent — which is the same fitted t0 that moves between runs. Note the direction: the pointing estimators want a smaller k and this bound wants a larger one, on the same arms. That disagreement is the thing to settle in October, and it argues against treating any single arm as the reference.

Flagged when a run's median sits at robust z ≥ 3.5 from its own arm's median and is shifted by at least 0.15 of that arm's track-level inter-quartile range. Both are required: several statistics agree so closely across runs that their across-run spread collapses, and a z alone then flags every run that differs at all. Runs with the most flags: run_126 (10), run_79 (5), run_156 (5), run_116 (3), run_81 (2).

run_145 has no per-tag granularity in this table. Its tracks were built from an already-merged August table and carry the literal tag prelim, so it has no timestamp, contributes nothing to the tag-level drift test, and is ordered here by run number rather than by clock. The condor full pass writes run_145 per tag like every other run, so this resolves when the table is rebuilt on it.

Spearman ρ of the per-tag median against the tag timestamp. Two columns, and the difference between them is the result: ρ over every tag, and ρ over the tags after the 27 July access only. A variable with a large all-tag ρ and a small post-access ρ stepped once at the access and then held. One with both is genuinely drifting.

The figures

What this does not rule out

  • It does not explain the angle scale. Nothing here moves run to run in a way that tracks k's 13–17 % scatter. The charge blow-up and D's degradation are real problems and are not, on this evidence, the cause of that scatter.
  • It cannot separate the chamber from the model. A chamber whose fit quality is poor and a forward model that does not describe that chamber look identical in every distribution here. Deciding between them needs the per-detector recalibration, not more QA.
  • The tag is a clock, not a condition. Two tags an hour apart share a timestamp neighbourhood but nothing guarantees they share a gas state, a threshold or an occupancy. A trend here is a correlation with time and not with a cause.
  • Chamber B is under-measured, not clean. Its distributions look tight because the quantities that would expose a problem — anything built on the angle — are null for every B track.
